chunks: What is a register. The question: What is a register?
A register is a small group of one-bit memories that share one clock and hold a multi-bit number together.
It keeps its value steady, then loads a new one at a clock tick when told to. Chips use registers between calculation steps, inside CPUs, and as control knobs for software.
Picture a row of eight light switches, each set to on (1) or off (0), plus a row of eight dials in front of them. A single lever, the clock, is wired to all eight switches.
When someone pulls the lever, every switch copies its dial at the same moment. Between pulls the switches hold still.
A lock on the lever, the load enable, decides whether a pull does anything.
Four flip-flops sit side by side.
Each D input takes one bit of the data bus, every clock pin (the small triangle input) is on the same CLK net, and the Q outputs together form the stored word.
All four bits update at the same clock edge.
Flip-flop: the one-bit memory that copies its input at a clock tick ("How a flip-flop or latch works"). A register is a row of them.
Clock tick: the repeating signal that says "capture now" ("Why digital systems need clocks"). Load enable: a control input.
The register only takes new data on ticks when it is on. Memory-mapped register: a register at an address that software can read or write to control a peripheral such as a timer.
Take an 8-bit register that starts at 0. The data input shows 0000 0101, which is 5. With load enable on, the next tick copies it, so the register holds 5.
Now the data input changes to 0000 1001, which is 9, but load enable is off. The next tick changes nothing, and the register still holds 5.
Turn load enable on, and the following tick loads 9. That is the whole idea.
"A register is a group of flip-flops sharing a clock that stores a multi-bit value: on the active edge, when enabled, all bits load together, and in between it holds.
An 8-bit register is eight D flip-flops.

In logic design it's the state between combinational stages; in a CPU it's the fast register file; a shift register moves bits along each clock; and in firmware, peripheral registers are memory-mapped addresses you read and write to configure and monitor hardware."
